description: Width tiers for English Year 8 — all 23 descriptors across Language, Literature and Literacy strands. One entry per descriptor code.
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest context or task that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For Language concept standards (LA): minimum engages one text type or language example. For Literature standards (LE): minimum analyses one literary text or produces one short literary text. For Literacy capability standards (LY): minimum applies the skill in one identified task context. Not the easiest version of the task — the honest floor for the command term.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor as ACARA intended. For Language standards: engages the range of language features, text types and contexts the descriptor specifies. For Literature standards: analyses or creates across the contexts indicated by elaborations. For Literacy capability standards: applies the skill across the range of task contexts elaborations suggest. Reflects sound standard classroom practice.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new text contexts, language phenomena, cultural perspectives or task types — not harder versions of the same task. First Nations directions included wherever elaborations indicate them. Some descriptors have genuinely thin width — these are flagged with 'Limited width' notes rather than padded with weak items.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as source data for determining typical scope and identifying First Nations, cultural and contextual directions. Not all elaborations are reproduced — they are synthesised where overlapping or used to infer reasonable wider directions within the year band.

AC9E8LA01.minimum_width: Identify language features (specialist terms or forms of address) in one social context that signal group membership.
AC9E8LA01.typical_width: Identify and explain how language features including specialist terminology, acronyms and terms of address create solidarity and define group identity across several social and cultural contexts — youth culture, sport and professional communities.
wider: Investigate how First Nations language names (AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia) reflect relationships to Country/Place and construct group and community identity
Compare how two contrasting groups use language differently to signal membership and manage relationships
Examine how language associated with an online community or subculture simultaneously includes insiders and excludes outsiders
elaborations: understanding that group identities are formed through language that reflects shared values, beliefs and behaviours, and through language choices that engender solidarity such as specialist terminology, acronyms and terms of address
exploring the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies Map of Indigenous Australia and identifying language names that inform relationships to Country/Place

AC9E8LA02.minimum_width: Identify one rhetorical device (irony or hyperbole) in a text and explain that the surface statement and implied meaning are different.
AC9E8LA02.typical_width: Identify and explain how irony, hyperbole, parody and understatement create a gap between literal statement and implied meaning across a range of texts including speeches, opinion pieces and humorous writing.
wider: Compare how two different devices achieve contrasting evaluative effects on the same subject in two different texts
Investigate how political cartoons or satirical writing use parody and irony simultaneously to layer multiple evaluative meanings
Examine how non-Western or First Nations rhetorical traditions use indirect or figurative expression to convey serious social or political commentary
elaborations: identifying how authors use rhetorical devices that reveal the dark or serious aspects of a topic in humorous or amusing ways; for example, by making a statement but implying or meaning the opposite (irony), exaggerating or overstating something (hyperbole), imitating or mocking something (parody), and making something appear less serious than it really is (understatement)

AC9E8LA03.minimum_width: Explain how the structure and at least two language features of one text type work together to achieve its purpose.
AC9E8LA03.typical_width: Explain how texts including critical responses, expositions, interpretations, discussions, literary recounts, memoirs, drama scripts, formal speeches and comparisons are structured and how their language features serve their communicative purposes; recognise how placement of images and text in online vs print texts affects meaning.
wider: Compare two texts with similar purposes but different structures and explain how structural variation affects meaning
Examine how formal speeches use structure and language features differently from written argument to achieve persuasive effect
Analyse how a complex hybrid text (e.g. creative nonfiction or personal essay) combines elements from multiple genres to achieve its purpose
Investigate how the non-linear structure of an online text creates different reading pathways and affects purpose
elaborations: recognising how texts such as critical responses to texts, expositions, text interpretations and discussions are typically structured to achieve their purpose
discussing how the placement of images and written text in a linear or non-linear way, such as online texts, is used differently in a variety of texts for a purpose

explaining the structure and language features of texts such as narratives, literary recounts, memoirs, drama scripts, types of poems, formal speeches, comparisons and creative responses, discussions and debates

AC9E8LA04.minimum_width: Identify the claim, example and substantiation in one paragraph and explain how they work together to develop the point.
AC9E8LA04.typical_width: Identify and explain how claims, examples, quotations and substantiation function together in extended analytical paragraphs; write paragraphs that explain, substantiate and exemplify a viewpoint.
wider: Compare a well-substantiated paragraph with one that makes a claim but lacks explanation, and analyse what is lost without the substantiation step
Examine how academic writing in different disciplines uses different conventions for substantiating claims
Annotate a published paragraph identifying each structural component and evaluating the substantiation's effectiveness
elaborations: writing paragraphs of extended length that explain, substantiate and exemplify a particular viewpoint

AC9E8LA05.minimum_width: Identify at least two embedded clauses in sentences and explain that they modify a noun phrase within the main clause.
AC9E8LA05.typical_width: Identify and explain how embedded clauses modify noun phrases to add information about people, places and things; distinguish defining from non-defining embedded clauses; use embedded clauses in own writing to add information concisely.
wider: Compare how embedded clause density differs between formal academic texts and informal spoken English, examining register implications
Examine how speechmakers use embedded clauses to present evaluative information as given rather than argued
Investigate how nominalisation and embedding work together to create high-density formal prose
elaborations: evaluating how speechmakers influence audiences though embedded clauses to add information
exploring how clauses and embedded clauses can be used to express ideas more succinctly

AC9E8LA06.minimum_width: Identify two nominalisations in an informative text and name the original verb or adjective form each was derived from.
AC9E8LA06.typical_width: Identify nominalisations across informative texts; explain the grammatical transformation; nominalise verbs in sentences and discuss the impact on tone, formality and abstraction for potential audiences.
wider: Compare nominalisation density across a newspaper report, academic article and informal blog on the same topic
Investigate how government or bureaucratic documents use nominalisation to create abstract, impersonal official language
Conduct critical reading of nominalisation to reveal hidden agency — how nominalisation removes actors and can have ideological effects in political writing
elaborations: highlighting examples of nominalisation in a range of texts including informative texts and explaining the impact on content and tone
nominalising relevant verbs in a series of sentences and discussing the impact of the change in tone on potential audiences

AC9E8LA07.minimum_width: Identify one intertextual reference in a visual text and explain what source text or cultural knowledge it draws on.
AC9E8LA07.typical_width: Identify and explain intertextual references in advertisements and other visual texts; explain how references depend on viewer knowledge; analyse how the interrelationship of words and images creates layered intertextual meaning.
wider: Compare two visual texts referencing the same source text and analyse how the same reference can be used to different effects
Investigate how visual parody relies on intertextual recognition for its comedy or critical effect
Examine how visual texts from different cultural contexts use intertextual references that may not translate across audiences
elaborations: identifying intertextual references in advertisements and discussing their impact on layering meaning; for example, the interrelationship of words and images

AC9E8LA08.minimum_width: Identify at least four academic vocabulary words in a provided text and explain that they are cross-disciplinary rather than subject-specific.
AC9E8LA08.typical_width: Identify academic vocabulary across texts on different topics; compare and contrast vocabulary choices considering how they create precise information or convey abstract ideas; use academic vocabulary accurately in own writing.
wider: Investigate how academic vocabulary differs across disciplines by comparing language in a science report, history essay and literary analysis
Compare academic vocabulary in a text for expert audiences vs one for a general audience on the same subject
Examine how students from language backgrounds other than English may have different relationships to academic vocabulary and what strategies support acquisition
elaborations: identifying the vocabulary of academic report writing on a topic; for example, the use of words such as 'evidence', 'consequence', 'contradiction' and 'acknowledge' for the topic 'sustainability'
comparing and contrasting vocabulary choices in academic texts, considering how they are used to create precise information or convey abstract ideas

AC9E8LA09.minimum_width: Identify one semicolon and one dash in provided texts and explain what function each performs.
AC9E8LA09.typical_width: Understand and explain conventions for using semicolons and dashes; use both marks in own writing across formal prose and creative/drama contexts; create dialogue showing interruptions, asides and pauses using dashes.
wider: Compare how semicolons suit formal register while dashes suit informal or creative writing and explain the register difference
Create dramatic dialogue using dashes deliberately to show interruptions, hesitations and pauses for character effect

Limited width — punctuation marks do not vary meaningfully across further contexts at this year band. Extension goes deeper: examining how cumulative punctuation choices across a text create a consistent authorial voice.
elaborations: creating dialogue in drama showing interruptions, asides and pauses for effect
AC9E8LA09.width_notes: depth_fallback used — semicolons and dashes are a narrow punctuation skill with limited contextual variation at this year band. Register contrast (formal semicolon vs informal dash) is the primary available enrichment direction.

AC9E8LE01.minimum_width: Explain how one idea or point of view in a literary text represents the values of an individual or group, connecting those values to a specific historical, social or cultural context.
AC9E8LE01.typical_width: Explain how ideas and points of view in literary texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors represent the values of individuals and groups in their historical, social and cultural contexts, including texts representing unique First Nations ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing.
wider: Explain how values in a text from a historical context differ from contemporary values about the same subject
Compare how the same historical period is represented by texts from different cultural perspectives, examining whose values each text prioritises
Examine how attitudes and ideas about the natural world in texts from non-Australian contexts differ from dominant Australian representations
elaborations: discussing representations of characters from historical contexts in literary texts; for example, discussing the romantic representation of the Australian swagman and the values it reflects
explaining attitudes and ideas about the natural world in literary texts drawn from contexts different to their own
explaining the ways texts by First Nations Australian authors represent unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing

AC9E8LE02.minimum_width: Identify language features, literary devices or text structures in one literary text and form an opinion about their contribution to style.
AC9E8LE02.typical_width: Identify and explain how combinations of language features, literary devices and text structures create the styles of literary texts; compare reviews or opinions about a text's style and evaluate those that challenge or support own views.
wider: Compare the styles of two literary texts from different periods or genres and evaluate which stylistic choices are most effective
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use distinct language features and structures to create styles drawing on cultural traditions not typically represented in mainstream criticism
Research critical responses to a literary text and evaluate how different critics have interpreted the same stylistic features differently
elaborations: comparing reviews of a literary text and evaluating opinions that challenge or support personal opinions
reflecting on and evaluating opinions and arguments about aspects of literary texts including characterisation, setting and plot

AC9E8LE03.minimum_width: Explain how at least two language or image choices in a text are designed to position the reader toward a particular response or viewpoint.
AC9E8LE03.typical_width: Explain how language and/or images position readers to respond and form viewpoints across a range of text types including picture books, film and print texts; share opinions about how texts position viewers to respond to characters.
wider: Analyse how a complex picture book combines words and images to position readers emotionally or morally
Analyse how a film positions the viewer to respond to a character using visual, audio and narrative choices
Compare how two texts on the same subject use different strategies to position readers toward opposing viewpoints
elaborations: discussing how a complex picture book combines words and images to position readers to respond
sharing opinions about how a film positions the viewer to respond to a character

AC9E8LE04.minimum_width: Identify one intertextual reference in a literary text and explain what source text it draws on and what the reference adds to understanding.
AC9E8LE04.typical_width: Identify intertextual references through allusion or quotation in literary texts; explain how knowledge of other texts influences understanding and appreciation of the aesthetic quality of the text being read.
wider: Investigate how a literary text uses allusions to a specific cultural tradition and examine what cultural knowledge that assumes of the reader
Examine how a contemporary author uses intertextual references to position their work within a literary tradition
Analyse how a parody or creative response to a canonical text generates aesthetic quality through the gap between original and imitation
elaborations: identifying intertextual references through allusion or quotation in written texts and discussing how knowledge of other texts influences the reader's understanding and appreciation

AC9E8LE05.minimum_width: Identify how one sentence-level choice (voice, syntax) creates a specific tone, and identify one image and explain the meaning it creates.
AC9E8LE05.typical_width: Analyse how sentence patterns including active/passive voice, simple and complex syntax, and sentence length create tone; analyse how imagery and related literary devices create meaning and effect across a range of literary texts.
wider: Compare how a short story writer and a poet create contrasting tones using different sentence structure approaches
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use sentence patterns that reflect oral storytelling rhythms to create tone distinct from Western prose tradition
Analyse how sustained imagery (extended metaphor or consistent image pattern) creates cumulative meaning across a literary text
elaborations: recognising that tone is influenced when an author uses active or passive voice
examining how writers use terse and relatively simple language choices or more elaborate and complex syntax, and how these influence meaning

recognising that First Nations Australian authors use words and language to set tone when writing or speaking about specific themes; for example, words used to set the tone when writing or speaking about Country/Place

AC9E8LE06.minimum_width: Create a short literary text that deliberately uses at least one literary device for a named effect, and explain the choice made.
AC9E8LE06.typical_width: Create and edit literary texts that experiment with multiple language features and literary devices for particular purposes and effects, including short stories with character-revealing dialogue, collaborative scripts and texts that combine multiple devices to evoke a reader response.
wider: Create a short story with a sustained dominant device and reflect on how the constraint shaped the writing
Collaborate with a peer to write and edit a short script focusing on dialogue choices for each character
Conduct a sustained editing cycle on a longer literary piece with a revision history documenting why each change was made
elaborations: creating short stories focusing on characters and dialogue
combining literary devices to evoke a reader response
collaborating with a peer, which may include using online spaces, to write a short script with 2 characters, focusing on dialogue choices for each character
editing the imagery and word choices when creating a literary text and reflecting on the effect of those changes

AC9E8LY01.minimum_width: Identify two features of a text (e.g. a social media post or speech) and explain how each reflects the context in which it was created.
AC9E8LY01.typical_width: Identify and explain how social media texts and speeches for reconciliation reflect the contexts in which they are created, examining how platform affordances, audience, purpose and historical moment are visible in textual features.
wider: Compare how a social media text and a formal speech on the same topic reflect different contextual constraints
Investigate how speeches for reconciliation reflect specific historical and political contexts through their language and structural choices
Examine how a First Nations community text reflects the specific cultural and political context of its creation
elaborations: identifying and explaining how social media texts reflect the context in which they are created
identifying how speeches for reconciliation reflect the context in which they are created

AC9E8LY02.minimum_width: In a discussion, use at least one interaction strategy (question, restatement or summary) to support or challenge a meaning expressed by another speaker.
AC9E8LY02.typical_width: Use a range of interaction strategies — clear speaking at appropriate length, probing questions about stated and implied ideas, restatement and summarising — to engage constructively in formal and informal discussion, including supporting or challenging meanings.
wider: Participate in a structured debate or Socratic discussion where the explicit goal is to challenge implied as well as stated meanings
Practise summarising an opposing speaker's argument accurately and fairly before challenging it
Reflect on own interaction patterns and evaluate how they affect the quality of discussion
elaborations: participating in pair, group, class, school and community speaking and listening situations, including informal conversations, discussions, debates and presentations
listening to a conversation or speech, identifying the point being made, and explaining the tone and manner of presentation
using effective strategies for dialogue and discussion in range of formal and informal contexts

AC9E8LY03.minimum_width: Analyse two language features in a text and evaluate whether they are effective for the text's purpose and audience, giving reasons.
AC9E8LY03.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate how language features vary according to purpose and audience; evaluate an author's use of sources and quotations and present a reasoned opinion about how well ideas are supported.
wider: Compare two authors addressing the same audience for the same purpose and evaluate which language approach is more effective
Investigate how the same source or quotation can support opposing claims depending on context and interpretation
Analyse how sources are selected and framed in a biased text — examining what source choices reveal about perspective and what sources are absent
elaborations: evaluating an author's use of language features to present an opinion about those features
evaluating the use of sources and quotations and presenting an opinion about how an author has supported an idea

AC9E8LY04.minimum_width: Identify the organisational structure used in one text and explain how that structure shapes what the reader understands.
AC9E8LY04.typical_width: Analyse how texts structured according to proposition/support, cause/effect, compare/contrast and problem/solution each shape meaning differently; determine the effectiveness of these structures for their purposes; analyse how a webpage's organisation shapes its meaning.
wider: Compare how a news article and academic essay organise the same information differently and analyse the effect on meaning and credibility
Rewrite a text section using a different organisational logic and analyse how the structural change shapes meaning
Analyse how a First Nations text organises knowledge relationally or through narrative, creating different kinds of meaning from Western logical structures
elaborations: identifying the structure of ideas in a range of texts
examining texts that structure ideas according to proposition and support, cause and effect, and compare and contrast, and determine their effectiveness
exploring texts that attempt to solve problems in a particular way
analysing how the organisation of a webpage shapes its meaning

AC9E8LY05.minimum_width: Apply at least two named comprehension strategies to a text and explain how they helped interpret or evaluate ideas — specifically what implied or inferred meaning they surfaced.
AC9E8LY05.typical_width: Use comprehension strategies to interpret and evaluate ideas in texts; apply criteria for evaluating website content; analyse the selection and composition of images for their effect on credibility of a text; connect and compare information across texts.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to a text from an unfamiliar cultural context and reflect on which strategies worked and what cultural knowledge gaps affected comprehension
Develop and apply explicit evaluation criteria for a class of texts (e.g. health websites) and systematically evaluate multiple texts
Investigate how cross-referencing information across texts can reveal inconsistencies between sources — and what to do when reliable sources disagree
elaborations: reflecting on content by connecting and comparing information across and between texts
determining and applying criteria for evaluating the content of a website
analysing the selection and composition of an image in a text and evaluating its effect on the credibility of the story

AC9E8LY06.minimum_width: Create a text for a specified purpose and audience that demonstrates at least two deliberate selection choices and can explain each; plan the text using a conceptual map or similar tool.
AC9E8LY06.typical_width: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts for a range of purposes (imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical) and audiences; select vocabulary to position and persuade; edit for grammar, spelling and punctuation accuracy and for meaning clarity.
wider: Create a text for an unfamiliar audience and reflect on what structural and language choices that audience requires
Conduct a systematic editing cycle with a revision history documenting why each editing decision was made
Create a multimodal text in which visual features and written text work interdependently, and reflect on how each modality contributes to overall purpose
elaborations: experimenting with and editing text structures and language features
selecting vocabulary to position and persuade the reader
editing for accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation, and for meaning
using conceptual maps or journals to plan and reflect on each stage of creating a written or multimodal text

AC9E8LY07.minimum_width: Deliver a spoken presentation demonstrating deliberate use of at least one voice feature (tone, volume, pitch or pace) for an intended effect.
AC9E8LY07.typical_width: Plan, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations for a range of purposes and audiences; select vocabulary, literary devices, visual features and voice features with deliberate attention to their effects; integrate multimodal features to support audience understanding.
wider: Deliver a debate speech using voice features and vocabulary deliberately to persuade and evaluate own performance
Create a voiceover for a media presentation, selecting voice features that complement visual elements
Collaborate to develop a persuasive advertising campaign about a contemporary issue, making explicit decisions about visual design, language and voice features
elaborations: integrating multimodal features in a spoken presentation to support the audience's understanding
choosing vocabulary and sentence structures, and using literary devices such as similes, metaphors and personification to meet perceived audience needs
selecting features of voice, such as tone, volume, pitch and pace, with particular attention to the effects these may have on audience reaction
collaborating with peers to develop a persuasive advertising campaign about a contemporary issue

AC9E8LY08.minimum_width: Apply morphemic knowledge to spell at least three complex words correctly, explaining how morpheme analysis guided the spelling.
AC9E8LY08.typical_width: Apply knowledge of morphemic patterns, etymology and unusual letter combinations to spell complex words across academic and creative writing; use appropriate sources (including AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia and local First Nations community guidance) to access correct spellings of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander language words.
wider: Investigate how words from particular language origins (Latin, Greek, French, Arabic) carry predictable morphemic patterns applicable to unfamiliar words
Explore how local First Nations community members are the authoritative source for correct spelling and pronunciation of community language words

Limited width — spelling is a skill with thin contextual variation at this year band. Extension goes deeper: using etymological research tools independently and developing strategies for learning large numbers of new words.
elaborations: understanding the different ways complex words are constructed, and drawing on morphemic knowledge and knowledge of unusual letter combinations when spelling these words

understanding where to obtain the spelling of Aboriginal language words and Torres Strait Islander language words; for example, the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies Map of Indigenous Australia, and the local First Nations Australian community
AC9E8LY08.width_notes: depth_fallback used alongside phenomena_contexts — spelling rules do not vary meaningfully across contexts, but the AIATSIS/First Nations source knowledge direction warrants specific coverage. Two standards are genuinely thin-width: LA09 and LY08.
